paras: The lynching of Chris Davis took place in Athens, Ohio, in the early hours of November 21, 1881, when a mob took Davis, a Black man described as a "mulatto," from the county jail and hanged him from the bridge over the Hocking River. Davis was awaiting the grand jury on a charge of assaulting an elderly widow near Albany, and the mob extracted a confession from him by promising to return him to jail. No one was arrested, and the case drew comment as a Northern lynching, with Ohio editors divided over it and women of Albany passing resolutions in its favor.

In early November papers reported that Mrs. Lucinda Luckey, a widow living alone near Albany in Athens County, had been "horribly maltreated" and her skull fractured, and that neighbors threatened to lynch the man arrested for it. Later accounts said Davis had broken down her door at about two in the morning, raped her and struck her with an ax, though they placed the attack anywhere from October 29 to November 5. Accounts of Davis himself differed: the Memphis Public Ledger said he had tended Mrs. Luckey's farm for years, while a Kentucky paper called him a Kentuckian who had moved to Ohio a few months earlier.
Because of the threats he was moved to the jail at Chillicothe for safety and was brought back to Athens shortly before the lynching to face the grand jury.

On the night of Sunday, November 20, a party of men from the Albany neighborhood, put at about twenty to about fifty, rode into Athens and posted guards at the houses of town officials and at the churches so that no alarm could be raised. According to the Ohio accounts, three of them gained entry by presenting one of their number as a captured horse thief, and seized Sheriff Warden when he opened the door. Finding no keys on him, they made other prisoners point out Davis's cell and broke its lock with a sledge hammer.

Davis was led with a rope around his neck about four blocks to the Hocking River bridge at the south edge of town, near the Ohio University. There he was told that if he confessed he would be taken back to jail and dealt with by law, and after he said "I'm the man" the crowd cried "Throw him off!" He was given three minutes to pray and then pushed from the bridge, and the nine-foot fall broke his neck; his body was found hanging there in the morning.

The coroner opened an inquest the same day, and the first dispatches said the mob had not been masked and would be arrested. By the end of January 1882, according to the Woodsfield Spirit of Democracy, the inquest had found that Davis died "at the hands of persons unknown to the jury" and no lynchers had been arrested, though some were said to be known throughout Albany and Athens.

At a meeting in Albany the ladies of the village resolved without dissent that Davis had met "a just and timelv fate," pledged to oppose the prosecution of anyone involved in the hanging, and asked the legislature to make rape a capital crime.

Papers across the country carried the Athens wire within a day, under headings such as "A Sheriff Overpowered" and "A Negro Lynched at Albany, O.," while the Cincinnati Gazette's account of the false promise ran as "How the Victim Was Betrayed into a Confession."

Ohio weeklies divided along partisan lines: the Somerset Press wrote that the lynchers had "rid the country of a brute," and the Eaton Democrat hoped no jury would convict any of them and called Davis "the black fiend and scoundrel." The Democratic Spirit of Democracy mocked Republican Athens, calling the act "a Northern Outrage," and later condemned the encouragement of mob law by the Athens Messenger and other papers.

Southern papers used the case to answer Northern criticism: a Maysville, Kentucky, paper said it showed "a bad state of society" in Ohio, and the Jackson Clarion noted Republican papers' shock at the lynching of "a negro ravisher in Ohio." The Charlotte Home and Democrat singled out the lynchers' false promise to Davis as "a dishonorable act."

The wire said the mob was not masked, and a syndicated brief called the men "undisguised," but Der Westbote and the Somerset Press described them as masked. Der Westbote alone said the sheriff's frightened wife threw down the jail keys, whereas other accounts said the lock was broken with a sledge. Most accounts place the hanging on the night of Sunday, November 20, but the Somerset Press and an Albany dispatch give the night of November 21.

reader.title: Lynching of Chris Davis
bases: A mob broke into the Athens jail, took out Chris Davis, a prisoner accused of assault, and hanged him from a bridge (A6, A9, A28).

Davis was taken from the sheriff's custody by a mob reported at twenty to fifty men and hanged from a bridge without trial (A9, A11, A20, A24); the mob acted on the accusation that he had assaulted Mrs. Luckey and extracted a confession before hanging him (A9, A28).

The Athens wire (A6, A9), the Gazette special (A5), and separate Ohio accounts in the Belmont Chronicle, Der Westbote, Jackson Standard and Somerset Press (A11, A13, A24, A28) agree on the jail break and the hanging from the Hocking River bridge.

accounts.gist: The sheriff was overpowered while the mob broke into the cell; Davis was found hanging from the Hocking River bridge; the mob was not masked and 'will be arrested'.

accounts.label: Cincinnati Gazette special
accounts.gist: On the bridge Davis was promised he would be returned to jail if he confessed; after he said 'I'm the man' he was given three minutes to pray and thrown off.

accounts.label: Ohio weekly accounts
accounts.gist: Masked men from Albany posted guards at officials' houses, gained entry by posing with a captured horse thief, broke the cell lock with a sledge and led Davis four blocks to the bridge.

accounts.label: Der Westbote (German, Columbus)
accounts.gist: Thirty to forty masked men threw the sheriff down; his wife, upstairs, threw down the keys in her fright.

framing.detail: Most papers outside Ohio carried the Athens wire under heads such as 'A Sheriff Overpowered', 'A Negro Lynched at Albany, O.' and 'A Mob's Vengeance'.
The Somerset Press said the lynchers 'rid the country of a brute'; the Eaton Democrat hoped no jury would convict and said hanging was 'too mild'.
The Democratic Spirit of Democracy first mocked Republican Athens for a 'Northern Outrage', then condemned the encouragement of mob law and the failure to arrest anyone.
Southern papers cited the lynching against Northern criticism of the South; the Charlotte Home and Democrat condemned the lynchers' lie to obtain a confession.

The assault was already reported in a paper dated November 5 (A2), which makes November 5 unlikely.
